protomire.headline: One model. Its whole lifecycle.
protomire.lead: A dedicated workbench for turning research and data into a model you can train, evaluate, and understand.
protomire.audience: For model builders who want their research, datasets, training recipes, evaluations, and exports to live in one connected workspace.
features: A project that follows the model
One workspace represents one model lifecycle. Research, immutable dataset versions, recipes, runs, and exports stay connected through model-version lineage.
Recipes you can inspect
Work with a typed graph or edit the recipe as JSON. Revisions, bounded iteration, conditions, and artifact ancestry preserve the structure of an experiment.
Humans and agents share the controls
The workbench and native MCP server use a shared authenticated operations service. External agents can work with the same project operations.
Know what training actually consumed
Dataset previews, consumption records, checkpoint evaluation, and functionality-family policies connect training runs to their data and evaluation results.
steps: Bring your research
Start a model project and organize source material, datasets, and the code it depends on.
Build the recipe
Choose training and evaluation components, configure resources, and retain a versioned recipe.
Run, compare, export
Inspect checkpoints and evaluation results, compare model versions, and prepare an export with its lineage intact.
protomire.example_title: A workspace organized around the model
protomire.example:
research/       Papers, citations, source material
datasets/       Registered versions and previews
recipe          Training + evaluation workflow
runs            Checkpoints, metrics, artifacts
model versions  Comparisons and lineage
exports         Reviewed publication bundles
protomire.example_note: Conceptual workspace map—not a required on-disk directory structure.
protomire.start: Protomire is in development. Start with the project quickstart and the installation-status page. Developers can build from source using the repository runbook.
protomire.status: Development builds exist for macOS and Linux with scoped acceptance. There is no published, signed, clean-machine-accepted release. Windows delivery is unfinished. First-party licensing has not yet been selected.

moonshiner.headline: Better training data starts with the whole trajectory.
moonshiner.lead: Author the tasks. Capture the work. Judge the result. Turn accepted model sessions into training data.
moonshiner.audience: For people building instruction-following, coding, and tool-use datasets who need more than a collection of final answers.
features: Start with seeds
Author tasks and choose the harnesses and models that generate and judge them.
Keep the development loop
Capture model trajectories, including tool interactions, corrections, and the steps that led to the result.
Judge before publishing
Independent review accepts or rejects traces. Rejected work can be retried before it enters the prepared dataset.
Keep the queues moving
Seed authoring, tracing, judging, formatting, privacy checks, local storage, and Hugging Face publication run as independent queues.
steps: Configure the roles
Choose author and judge models, providers, project storage, and publication preferences.
Generate and review
Run enabled queues and inspect accepted traces, rejections, retries, and throughput.
Prepare and publish
Format accepted trajectories for training and publish to your configured Hugging Face dataset.
moonshiner.example_title: From installation to the first run
moonshiner.example:
python3 -m pip install moonshiner
moonshiner

# Inspect the active project
moonshiner status
moonshiner doctor
moonshiner.example_note: The first run opens setup. Model providers may require credentials and incur their own usage costs.
moonshiner.start: Install Moonshiner, run the setup assistant, and select your author and judge roles. Start with a small project and inspect the accepted traces before scaling up.
moonshiner.status: Pi and Codex can author traces and seeds. Claude Code is supported as a judge. Provider access, credentials, and upstream terms depend on your selected configuration.

jev-graph-builder.headline: Give your documents connections worth retrieving.
jev-graph-builder.lead: Build a searchable knowledge graph where proposed facts and relationships are checked before they enter the graph.
jev-graph-builder.audience: For teams turning a document collection into cited assistant context, graph retrieval, or training examples.
features: Documents become a graph
Split source material into chunks, extract entities and facts, create summaries, and connect related passages.
A proposal and a check
Claude Code or Codex drafts the text. Jev answers typed questions that gate what is accepted.
Retrieve beyond similar words
Vector search finds relevant passages; graph links lead to related context. The MCP server returns source citations to assistants.
Keep the evidence trail
Passages, facts, and relationships trace back to the source material and the decisions that accepted them.
steps: Choose the corpus
Point the builder at supported documents or folders, and review the proposed ontology.
Build and audit
Extract, embed, merge, link, and audit through the staged pipeline.
Put the graph to work
Query it through MCP or export Q&A and fact sets for model training.
jev-graph-builder.example_title: Build a graph from your documents
jev-graph-builder.example:
pip install jev-graph-builder

# Configure your TypeSafe key in your environment
# Start a build with Claude Code
jev-graph-builder --harness claude_code build ./my-docs
jev-graph-builder.example_note: Requires Python 3.11+, a configured System One service, an authenticated coding agent, and PostgreSQL with pgvector or a supported container runtime.
jev-graph-builder.start: Install the package, configure the decision-model service, and select a document folder. The builder pauses for approval of its initial ontology; interrupted builds can be resumed.
jev-graph-builder.status: The default decision service is TypeSafe’s Jev. Other System One endpoints can be configured. Model and provider usage are separate from the local graph tooling.

jev-no-bullshit.headline: “All tests pass.” Did they actually run?
jev-no-bullshit.lead: Check an AI coding assistant’s final summary against the actions and evidence in its session.
jev-no-bullshit.audience: For anyone who wants an assistant’s completion report to distinguish verified work, failures, and unfinished tasks.
features: Catch unverified claims
Look for statements such as “all tests pass” when the session provides no matching evidence.
Make uncertainty explicit
Flag weasel words that soften a claim without explaining what was checked.
Surface omitted failures
Detect summaries that leave out a failed command or unfinished step while presenting the overall work as complete.
Ask for a grounded correction
When a summary fails the check, the assistant receives specific feedback and can verify the work or correct its report.
steps: Configure Jev
Install the plugin for your assistant and supply a TypeSafe API key through its documented configuration.
Work normally
The check runs when the assistant produces its final summary.
Review the correction
Flagged claims are returned to the assistant with reasons tied to the session evidence.
jev-no-bullshit.example_title: The kind of claim it checks
jev-no-bullshit.example:
Assistant: “All tests are passing.”

Session evidence: no test command was run.

Feedback: Verify the claim against recorded actions,
or state plainly that tests were not run.
jev-no-bullshit.example_note: Illustrative example. A model-based check is not a guarantee that every incorrect claim will be detected.
jev-no-bullshit.start: Choose the installation instructions for Claude Code, Codex, pi, or OpenCode. Configure the key in the plugin’s own protected configuration file and approve the hook where your host requires it.
jev-no-bullshit.status: Supports Claude Code, Codex, pi, and OpenCode. Requires Python 3.10+ and TypeSafe service access. Host-specific behavior and retry limits are documented in the repository.

jev-scope-control.headline: Keep the next tool call inside the agreement.
jev-scope-control.lead: A scope check at the point where an assistant is about to act.
jev-scope-control.audience: For users of coding assistants who want proposed tool calls checked against the work they actually requested or agreed to.
features: Check before execution
A PreToolUse hook evaluates the proposed tool call before it proceeds.
Use the agreed scope
Jev assesses the call in relation to the user’s request and agreement.
Give a reason
Out-of-scope calls are denied with an explanation that the assistant can act on.
steps: Review the integration
Choose the host integration and inspect its configuration and examples.
Define the work
Give your assistant a clear task and constraints.
Check proposed actions
The hook submits the proposed call for a scope decision and denies it when outside the agreement.
jev-scope-control.example:
Agreed task: inspect a failing test.
Proposed action: change an unrelated deployment.

The hook checks whether that action belongs
to the work the user requested or approved.
jev-scope-control.example_note: Illustrative scenario—not a recorded decision or a live model response.
jev-scope-control.start: Review the repository’s host integrations, examples, and configuration before enabling the hook in your assistant. The integration files are the current setup reference.
jev-scope-control.status: Uses TypeSafe’s Jev for scope judgments. This is a model-based control; review host behavior and the repository tests when adopting it.

triggerfish.headline: Your agent. Across your channels. Under your policies.
triggerfish.lead: A multi-channel AI agent platform with a deterministic policy layer beneath the language model.
triggerfish.audience: For people who want an assistant connected to their messaging and tools, with explicit rules for information flow.
features: Meet the agent where you work
Connect through supported messaging channels, WebChat, or the command line.
Enforce policy in code
Classification gates and deterministic hooks govern what the agent can read, do, and send.
Choose your model provider
Configure supported hosted providers or local models, with provider choices independent of the messaging interface.
Extend through The Reef
Discover skills and plugins, or build capabilities for your own workflows.
steps: Install and configure
Follow the installation guide and use the setup wizard.
Connect channels and models
Choose your providers, channels, and policy configuration.
Work with your agent
Use its tools and skills within the configured information-flow boundaries.
triggerfish.example:
Channels → Gateway → Agent loop
                    ↕
           Deterministic policy
                    ↕
              Tools & skills
triggerfish.example_note: Conceptual platform overview. Full architecture and security documentation are on trigger.fish.
triggerfish.start: The Triggerfish website is the primary destination for installation, architecture, channel integrations, and usage guides.
triggerfish.status: Apache 2.0 source. Provider usage and optional managed services have their own requirements and terms.

fabletron.headline: A model experiment you can inspect from data to evaluation.
fabletron.lead: Fabletron brings Nemotron fine-tuning, exported weights, and evaluation tooling into one inspectable project.
fabletron.audience: For researchers exploring agentic coding, planning, and tool use on a hybrid Nemotron model.
features: Fine-tuning recipe
QLoRA training on the pi_agent split of Fable-5 traces targets agentic behavior and tool use.
Published weight formats
Choose among LoRA, BF16, GGUF, NVFP4, and MLX artifacts for different research and runtime paths.
Compare with the base
The evaluation harness reports differences against the base across instruction-following, reasoning, coding, and function-calling benchmarks.
steps: Choose a format
Match the model artifact to the runtime and hardware you intend to use.
Inspect the model card
Review architecture requirements, provenance, and licensing before download.
Run and evaluate
Use the documented serving path and compare results for your own workloads.
fabletron.example:
LoRA     Apply the fine-tune delta
BF16     Full-precision merged weights
GGUF     Compatible llama.cpp / LM Studio
NVFP4    NVIDIA Blackwell serving
MLX      Apple Silicon workflows
fabletron.example_note: Runtime support and memory requirements differ. See each artifact’s model card.
fabletron.start: Start with the source repository for evaluation tooling, or choose a model format below. The source README documents the Mac and Linux paths separately.
fabletron.status: Research artifacts derived from an upstream base model and dataset. The combined upstream license conditions apply; the model cards describe them.

reef-registry.headline: A place for Triggerfish capabilities to grow.
reef-registry.lead: The Reef is the public registry for discovering and sharing Triggerfish skills and plugins.
reef-registry.audience: For Triggerfish users looking for capabilities and contributors who want to publish their own.
features: Discover skills and plugins
Static catalogs describe available packages, versions, tags, and metadata.
Contribute through GitHub
Submit a pull request with a versioned skill or plugin and the required metadata.
Validate before publication
Repository checks validate submissions and rebuild the published JSON indexes.
steps: Find or create a capability
Browse the catalogs or prepare a versioned package.
Submit it for review
Follow the contribution instructions and open a pull request.
Publish to the registry
Accepted submissions become part of the generated static indexes.
reef-registry.example:
Skills   → catalog, tags, categories
Plugins  → catalog, tags, categories
Versions → metadata + package content
reef-registry.example_note: Registry structure summarized from its public source.
reef-registry.start: Browse the repository’s contribution and review guidance. Use Triggerfish for discovery and installation in your own environment.
reef-registry.status: A static registry served through GitHub Pages. Individual packages retain their own metadata and requirements.

triggerfish-cms-auth.headline: Give your CMS the missing authentication bridge.
triggerfish-cms-auth.lead: GitHub OAuth endpoints for Decap CMS sites hosted on Cloudflare Pages.
triggerfish-cms-auth.audience: For website maintainers using Decap CMS outside Netlify who need a server-side GitHub authentication flow.
features: Cloudflare Functions endpoints
Run the OAuth bridge alongside your Pages project.
Decap CMS configuration
Start from the included admin configuration and point it at your own site.
A focused integration
Connect the CMS, GitHub OAuth application, and deployment environment without a separate full application server.
steps: Register OAuth
Create the GitHub OAuth application for your site.
Configure secrets
Store the client ID and secret in your hosting environment.
Deploy and sign in
Add the Functions and admin files, configure the CMS, and test the login flow.
triggerfish-cms-auth.example:
Decap CMS → GitHub OAuth
                ↕
     Cloudflare Functions
                ↕
       Your site repository
triggerfish-cms-auth.example_note: Use your own OAuth application and deployment configuration. Never put client secrets in browser code.
triggerfish-cms-auth.start: Follow the repository setup guide for OAuth registration, Cloudflare configuration, and the CMS admin files.
triggerfish-cms-auth.status: Based on community Netlify CMS OAuth work and adapted to Cloudflare Functions. A starter configuration still needs site-specific setup.

tq_data_requirements.headline: An ESXi inventory without the manual collection.
tq_data_requirements.lead: Collect host hardware and configuration data over SSH with a PowerShell script built for multiple hosts.
tq_data_requirements.audience: For infrastructure engineers gathering repeatable ESXi inventory and configuration evidence.
features: Collect across hosts
Read a host list and run the collection concurrently within the configured throttle.
Handle interrupted work
Retries and resume support reduce repeated collection after a failure.
Capture useful hardware detail
Gather version, BIOS, CPU, memory, storage, networking, and driver information into CSV output.
steps: Prepare the environment
Install PowerShell 7+, VMware PowerCLI, and Posh-SSH.
List the hosts
Create a host file and choose concurrency, retry, and SSH-state options.
Collect and review
Run the script and inspect the resulting inventory CSV.
tq_data_requirements.example_note: PowerShell command; use one line when running it. Requires authorized host access and the modules documented in the repository.
tq_data_requirements.start: Install the required modules and review the SSH behavior before running against your authorized hosts. The README lists every supported option and collected field.
tq_data_requirements.status: PowerShell 7+ with VMware PowerCLI and Posh-SSH. Host permissions, connectivity, and SSH configuration determine what can be collected.

vcf-9-x-skills.headline: The right VCF answer starts with the right version.
vcf-9-x-skills.lead: 28 agent skills for VMware Cloud Foundation 9.0, 9.1, and 9.1.1. Documented endpoints, prerequisites, and workflows—organized for the version you actually run.
vcf-9-x-skills.audience: For infrastructure engineers using coding assistants to research, plan, and automate VMware Cloud Foundation operations.
features: Settle the version first
Version-scoped reference files keep 9.0, 9.1, and 9.1.1 facts separate. Skills ask for the version or distinguish the answers instead of guessing.
Cover the operational stack
NSX, vSphere, vSAN, VKS, SDDC Manager, VCF Automation, Operations, PowerCLI, backup, recovery, licensing, and lifecycle workflows.
Bring Dell context along
Includes documented OMEVV, iDRAC, and PowerFlex SDC two-layer infrastructure integrations.
Install for your assistant
Download ready-to-use packages for Windsurf, Claude, Codex, Triggerfish, or OpenClaw. No build step is needed.
steps: Choose your tool
Download the ZIP for your assistant and extract its skill folders.
Copy the skills
Place them in the documented project or user skills directory for that tool.
Ask with a version
State which VCF release you use. The skills route to the appropriate references and cite their evidence.
vcf-9-x-skills.example_title: Questions these skills are built for
vcf-9-x-skills.example:
“What are the prerequisites for our VCF upgrade?”

“Block RDP between app-tier and db-tier in NSX 9.1.”

“Show the SDDC Manager token flow for 9.0.”
vcf-9-x-skills.example_note: Example prompts. The published material was checked against documentation and specifications, not run against a live VCF deployment.
vcf-9-x-skills.start: Download the package for your assistant, copy the skills into its documented location, and follow the repository’s installation checks. Triggerfish requires copies rather than symlinks.
vcf-9-x-skills.status: MIT-0. Documentation-derived coverage for VCF 9.0, 9.1, and 9.1.1. Published evaluations predate the October update; no live-environment validation is claimed.

kimi-k3-trace-explorer.headline: Kimi K3 Trace Explorer
kimi-k3-trace-explorer.lead: Browse, search, and export agentic coding trajectories.
kimi-k3-trace-explorer.audience: For anyone who wants to inspect agent trajectories before using them in a training workflow.
features: What this repository contains
A Gradio interface with dataset summaries, trajectory minimaps, syntax-highlighted tool calls, edit diffs, and filtered JSONL export. Open the Space to check its current runtime availability.
Inspect sessions visually
Use the explorer’s summaries, trajectory minimaps, highlighted code, and edit diffs to understand a session.
Find and export
Search for patterns and export filtered subsets as JSONL through the Space’s interface.
